Fit the regression models for separable treatment effects

Source: R/fit.R
biscal.Rd

Fits, by maximum likelihood, the four baseline-category logistic regression models through which the separable treatment effects of Hu and Yi (2026) are identified: the transition models for the two responses (model (12) of the paper) and the models for their baseline values (models (13) and (14)). Intermittent missingness and right-censoring are handled as in Section 4 of the paper.

Usage

biscal(formula, data, id, time, treatment, control = list())

Arguments

formula

A formula cbind(y1, y2) ~ x1 + x2 + .... The left-hand side names the two responses, the one measured first at each visit first. They may be numeric (the sorted distinct values are the ordered categories), logical, or factors (ordered or not; the level order is used). The right-hand side lists baseline covariates, which may include factors, interactions and transformations such as scale() or poly() (evaluated on new covariate values with the parameters of the fitted data); use ~ 1 for none. offset() terms are not supported.

data

A data frame in long format: one row per subject and visit.

id, time, treatment

Names (strings) of the columns of data holding the subject identifier, the visit index (0 for the baseline visit, 1, ..., K for the scheduled follow-up visits) and the treatment. The treatment may be coded 0/1, logical, or a two-level factor whose first level is the control group. The treatment and covariates must be constant within subjects.

control

A list of convergence settings: epsilon (relative change in the log-likelihood, default 1e-8) and maxit (maximum number of iterations, default 25; at least 100 are allowed for responses with more than two categories).

Value

An object of class "biscal", a list with components including

coefficients

List of the four coefficient matrices beta1, beta2, gamma1 and gamma2 (terms in rows, categories \(d = 1, \dots, L - 1\) in columns).

vcov

Block-diagonal covariance matrix of all coefficients (inverse observed information), in the order of coef.biscal().

K

The last visit index \(K\), the default end time point of the effects.

n, nobs_models, loglik

Number of subjects, number of observations used by each model and the maximized log-likelihood.

X, A, covariate_data

Subject-level covariate matrix (used by easte() by default), treatment and covariate values.

and information on the data used by the methods.

Model

For subject \(i\) at visit \(k = 0, 1, \dots, K\), let \(Y_{1,k}\) and \(Y_{2,k}\) be the two responses, with \(Y_{1,k}\) measured before \(Y_{2,k}\); let \(A\) be the treatment and \(X\) the baseline covariates. With \(D_j(\cdot)\) the dummy (indicator) coding of a previous response, the models are, for every category \(d \ge 1\):

  • beta1 (model (12), \(j = 1\)): \(\log\{P(Y_{1,k} = d \mid \cdot)/P(Y_{1,k} = 0 \mid \cdot)\} = \beta_{1,0,d} + \beta_{1,1,d}^\top D_1(y_{1,k-1}) + \beta_{1,2,d}^\top D_2(y_{2,k-1}) + \beta_{1,3,d}\, a + \beta_{1,4,d}^\top x\);

  • beta2 (model (12), \(j = 2\)): the same with \(D_1(y_{1,k})\), the first response at the same visit, in place of \(D_1(y_{1,k-1})\);

  • gamma1 (model (13)): \(Y_{1,0}\) given \(x\);

  • gamma2 (model (14)): \(Y_{2,0}\) given \(D_1(y_{1,0})\) and \(x\).

The transition models are common to all visits \(k \ge 1\). Binary responses give ordinary logistic regressions. Every category of each response must occur as an outcome of each model (for example, a response cannot be constant at baseline), and the visits must be numbered consecutively so that transitions between visits \(k - 1\) and \(k\) are observed.

Missing data and censoring

Responses that are not observed are coded NA, or their rows are omitted (for example, all visits after a subject is censored). Following Section 4.2 of the paper, the transition of the first response at visit \(k\) contributes to the likelihood when \(Y_{1,k}\), \(Y_{1,k-1}\) and \(Y_{2,k-1}\) are observed, and that of the second response when \(Y_{2,k}\), \(Y_{2,k-1}\) and \(Y_{1,k}\) are observed (the indicators \(m'_{i,j,k}\) of the paper). This is valid when missingness and censoring satisfy Conditions AC1 and AC2 of the paper (for example, when they depend only on the treatment, the covariates and earlier responses). The baseline models use the subjects whose baseline responses are observed.

References

Hu, P. and Yi, G. Y. (2026). Inference about separable causal effects with longitudinal bivariate ordinal responses with missingness and censoring. Statistics in Medicine, 45, e70320. doi:10.1002/sim.70320

See also

biscal-methods for summary(), coef() and other methods; aste() and easte() for the separable treatment effects and tests.

Examples

fit <- biscal(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x1 + x2, data = simtrial, id = "id",
              time = "visit", treatment = "trt")
fit
#> Separable treatment effects for longitudinal bivariate responses (BiSCaL)

#> Call:
